ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *ganganąder.? Proto-Germanic *gagin Proto-Germanic *in gagin Proto-West Germanic *in gagin Old English onġēan Middle English agayn English again From Middle English agayn, from Old English onġēan (“against, again”), from Proto-West Germanic *in gagin, from Proto-Germanic *in gagin. Cognate with German entgegen (“contrary to”), North Frisian ijen (“against”), Danish igen (“again”), Swedish igen (“again”), and Norwegian Bokmål igjen (“again”), and Icelandic í gegnum (“through”). By surface analysis, on- + gain (“against”).

senses.d: Another time: indicating a repeat of an action.
ex: I enjoyed it so much I went again the next day.
He tangled in tree-tops again and again / And barely missed hitting a tri-motored plane.

senses.d: Back (to a former place or state).
ex: We need to bring the old customs to life again.
The South will rise again.

senses.d: Over and above a factor of one.
ex: This stick is quite long, but that other one is half as long again.

senses.d: Used metalinguistically, with the repetition being in the discussion, or in the linguistic or pragmatic context of the discussion, rather than in the subject of discussion.
ex: Great, thanks again!

senses.d: Tell me again, say again; used in asking a question to which one may have already received an answer that one cannot remember.
ex: What's that called again?

senses.d: I ask again, I say again; used in repeating a question or statement.
ex: Again, I'm not criticizing, I just want to understand.

senses.d: Here too, here also, in this case as well; used in applying a previously made point to a new instance; sometimes preceded by "here".
ex: Approach B is better than approach A in many respects, but again, there are difficulties in implementing it.

senses.d: Back in the reverse direction, or to an original starting point.
ex: Bring us word again.
And after they were warned in ther slepe, that they shulde not go ageyne to Herod, they retourned into ther awne countre another way.

senses.d: In return, as a reciprocal action; back.
ex: So women are never angrie, but to the end a man should againe be angrie with them, therein imitating the lawes of Love.
Thus men are plagued with women, they again with men, when they are of diverse humours and conditions[…].

senses.d: In any other place.
ex: There is not, in the world again, such a spring and seminary of brave military people as in England, Scotland, and Ireland.

senses.d: Against.
ex: You may think you are all on the same side, agin the government.
And here begynneth the treson of Kynge Marke that he ordayned agayne Sir Trystram.

grp.label: back to a former place or state
used in a question to ask something one has forgotten

ety.text: Compare Latin denuo and de novo.
Probably from Old French ancor, from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare Catalan and Occitan encara, Italian ancora. Sense 5 is a semantic loan from German noch (adverb).

From Latin dē (“from”) + novō (“new”), possibly a restructured inherited form of Classical Latin dēnuō (“again, anew”), itself a reduced form of a supposed and unattested Old Latin *dē novōd. Related to Medieval Latin dē novō (“afresh, as a new thing, out of nowhere”). Compare Old Spanish de nuevo, Romanian din nou.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hancōra, probably from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare French encore, Occitan and Catalan encara.
From Latin re-. The prefix ri- is inherited from Latin, while the variant re- is borrowed from Latin.

es:otra vez.gl: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see otra, vez.

ety.text: Literally, “another time”.

Inherited from Old Spanish de nuevo (“again”), from Latin dē (“from”) + novō (“new”), possibly a restructured inherited form of Classical Latin dēnuō (“again, anew”), itself a reduced form of a supposed and unattested Old Latin *dē novōd. Related to Medieval Latin dē novō (“afresh, as a new thing, out of nowhere”).
From nueva + -mente.
Borrowed from Latin dē novō (“anew”).
outra (“another”) + vez (“time”)
From nova + -mente.

pt:de volta.gl: back (to or in a previous condition or place)

ety.text: From Middle French desia, from Old French des ja corresponding to dès + jà.

chain.g: used as an intensifier of substantive and less frequently adjective personal pronouns, usually followed by ipse

ety.text: From Old Galician-Portuguese mesmo, from earlier Old Galician-Portuguese meesmo, from Vulgar Latin of Iberia *medesmo, from proto-Romanic forms as *medessimu, from *medissimu, from *medipsimu, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from a previous *metipsissīmus, derived from Latin -met (emphatic suffix) + ipse (“himself”) + -…

Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-der. Proto-Germanic *ganganąder.? Proto-Germanic *gagin Proto-Germanic *in gagin Proto-West Germanic *in gagin Old English onġēander. Middle English ayenes English against Formed from Middle English ayenes, agenes, againes (“in opposition to”), a southern variant of agen, or directly from again, either way with adverbial genitive singular ending -es; the parasitic -t was added circa 1350, probably by confusion with the superlative ending -est. By surface analysis, again + -st (excrescent ending).

senses.d: In a contrary direction to.
ex: It is hard work to swim against the current.

senses.d: In physical opposition to; in collision with.
ex: The rain pounds against the window.

senses.d: In physical contact with, so as to abut or be supported by.
ex: The ladder was leaning against the wall.
The puppy rested its head against a paw.

senses.d: Close to, alongside.
ex: A row of trees stood against a fence.

senses.d: In front of; before (a background).
ex: The giant was silhouetted against the door.

senses.d: In contrast or comparison with.
ex: He stands out against his classmates.
This report sets out the risks against the benefits.

senses.d: In competition with, versus.
ex: The Tigers will play against the Bears this weekend.

senses.d: Contrary to; in conflict with.
ex: Doing this is against my principles.
It is against the law to smoke on these premises.

senses.d: In opposition to.
ex: His mind is closed against all arguments.
Are you against freedom of choice?

senses.d: Of betting odds, denoting a worse-than-even chance.
ex: That horse is fifty-to-one against, so it has virtually no chance of winning.

senses.d: By the time that (something happened); before.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French contre, from Old French contre, from Latin contra.
Borrowed from Latin contrārius.
Inherited from Old Italian contra, from Latin contrā.
Inherited from Latin contrā. Old Spanish had cuentra as well, with diphthongization of stressed Latin /ŏ/. As the word was generally atonic, the unstressed variant contra prevailed over time.
Proto-Italic *komterosder. Proto-Italic *komterād Latin contrā Portuguese contra Inherited from Latin contrā.

es:cerca de.gl: close to, near, near to, around, close by
